The missed call: An electrician’s afternoon

  1. A customer needs an electrician. Jamie reads the electrical repairs page and chooses Contact now.
  2. The phone rings. Your hands are full. Jamie calls while you are working. The call is missed.
  3. They hear back without waiting for you. Automatic reply: Thanks for calling Current Electric. Sorry we missed you. What can we help with? Jamie: The kitchen outlets stopped working this morning. Can someone take a look?
  4. A useful conversation is waiting. Your inbox contains Jamie’s reply and the kitchen outlet problem. It is ready for you to respond.
  5. You handle the advice and the arrangements. You: Thanks, Jamie. I’ll call you to discuss the issue and the next step. Jamie: Thanks. I’m available this afternoon. The owner confirms availability, assessment, and costs.
  6. Less phone tag. A clearer starting point. The customer is acknowledged, the problem is described, and you choose the next step. Rules and handoff are agreed during setup.

Why it helps: A customer to call back. A useful description of the job.

The roof inquiry: A homeowner after the rain

  1. A damp patch sends Alex looking for help. Alex finds the roof-repair page and selects Request an assessment after noticing a damp patch.
  2. A few details. No roofing vocabulary needed. Alex Example selects Roof repair and writes: A damp patch above the upstairs window after rain. The website receives the request.
  3. The request gets an acknowledgment. Automatic reply: Thanks, Alex. We’ve received your roof-repair request. When did you first notice the damp patch?
  4. Alex adds the part you would ask anyway. Alex replies: After Monday’s rain. We haven’t noticed a leak there before. This background is added to the inquiry.
  5. Now you can arrange the right next step. The team reviews Alex’s inquiry and confirms access, assessment charges, and timing directly. Automation does not confirm an appointment.
  6. A prepared conversation, before the visit. The customer has selected a service and supplied useful details. Your team handles the assessment and recommendation.

Why it helps: The request arrives with details your team can use.

After the job: A plumbing job, finished

  1. The repair is done. Start with that. Your team marks Sam’s sink repair complete. This is the agreed starting point for a review invitation.
  2. A thank-you, with a simple invitation. Review invitation: Thanks for choosing Clearflow, Sam. Would you share an honest review of your experience? A direct review link follows.
  3. One link to the review page. Sam can choose any rating. Feedback is optional, and invitations do not filter customers by satisfaction.
  4. If needed, one useful nudge. An optional reminder follows under the agreed timing and stopping rules, inviting Sam to share their experience.
  5. A reply or opt-out stops the sequence. A reply or opt-out stops automated reminders under the agreed rules. Your team handles personal replies.
  6. Good work. A consistent way to ask. The invitation uses a direct link and agreed timing. It supports asking without promising reviews or particular ratings.

Why it helps: An easy, consistent way to invite honest feedback.

Getting your website: From your idea to launch

  1. Start with the business you already know. Share your business name, services, area, and a website example you like. No technical brief is required.
  2. Know what you’re getting before we build. We agree the page plan, content responsibilities, scope, costs, and terms together before building.
  3. Open your website. Click through it. You open the draft website, check the pages and contact flow, and request refinements before launch.
  4. Make the messages sound like you. You approve the message wording, timing, stopping rules, and where customer replies reach you.
  5. Follow a sample inquiry all the way through. We check the mobile pages, navigation, forms, sample inquiries, replies, and the agreed owner handoff.
  6. Go live when the details are right. After you approve the website, messages, and publishing details, launch follows the agreed plan. Ongoing responsibilities are confirmed.

Why it helps: You can review the website and the replies before anything goes live.

The practical details

Here’s what
you’re getting.

We plan the pages and messages around your business, then agree on the scope together.

0110–20 page business website

A professional, mobile-friendly website with 10–20 pages to explain your services, answer common questions, and help customers get in touch.

  • 10–20 pages, planned around your business
  • Clear service pages and inquiry forms
  • Designed for phones, tablets, and computers
02Automatic inquiry follow-up

A follow-up sequence acknowledges new inquiries and helps keep the conversation moving while you are busy running your business.

  • An initial reply to a new inquiry
  • Follow-up messages tailored to your business
  • A clear handoff when it is time for you to respond
03Missed-call text replies

When you cannot answer, an automatic text lets the caller know you missed them and invites them to explain what they need.

  • An automatic reply after a missed call
  • A message that sounds like your business
  • An easy way for the customer to reply
04Review requests & reminders

Send a clear invitation to review your business after a completed job, with reminders that help customers follow through.

  • A straightforward review invitation
  • Follow-up reminders for eligible customers
  • The same opportunity to leave honest feedback for everyone
05On-page SEO foundations

Clear page titles, useful service content, and accurate business information give your website a sensible foundation for search.

  • Unique page titles and descriptions
  • Clear headings, service content, and internal links
  • Structured information using your verified business details
